Its not too hard to get your head around. Start by understanding that some kinds of em waves can pass through some kinds of solid matter. For example X-rays pass through your flesh and cloths, radio waves pass through your houses walls, gamma rays pass through almost everything, etc. Next understand that all types of em radiation (visible light, radio and microwaves, x-rays and so on) are all caused by the same force carrying particle, the photon, but at different energy levels, and oscillating at different frequencies.

The reason visible light tends not to pass through most objects is because photons in the visible spectrum are easily absorbed by most atomic structures. In order for light to pass through unobstructed the type of matter must be "full" IE there is no place for photons to get absorbed. I don't have a complete understanding of this, but as far as I do understand the outermost electron shell of the matter in question, must be completely full, either because it is full in its pure elemental state, or because it is filled by sharing electrons in a chemical bond. Feel free to correct me if I'm not 100% accurate on this.

Now lets look at an example, everyday carbon. Carbon comes many forms, from completely opaque graphite to highly transparent diamond. Why is that you ask? Its all about how the carbon is bonded to itself. In the case of graphite, the carbon atoms are bound "loosely" or to put it another way not all the possible bonding points are used. Think of a ball with 6 magnetic attachment points, 1 in each cardinal direction. Now think of how strong a block of these balls would be if an average of only 2 or 3 of the anchor points were attached on each ball. This is graphite, weak enough you can crush it in your hand, and each magnet that isn't used to anchor a ball is free to absorb a passing photon. Now think about these same balls, but with each and every anchor point connected to the ball next to it, forming an orderly lattice. This is diamond, extremely strong, and with no unused anchor points for photons to fall into, so the light simply passes through undisturbed.
